publicationStmt.p: Editorial revision 1.2, approved 31 October 2026. This book incorporates 0 approved running-text revisions and 1 new translation-comparison note from the Pollard–Lauro comparison. Across the five books, the release incorporates three running-text revisions and three new comparison notes. Two revisions adopt Lauro’s interpretation; the third follows reconsideration of the Latin. Earlier publication statements below preserve the version 1.1 and version 1.0 history. Every other running passage, all previous comparison notes and all citation identifiers remain unchanged. See _docs/LAURO_ENGLISH_V1_2_RELEASE_20261031.md.

Editorial revision 1.1, approved 25 October 2026, supersedes version 1.0 only at the designated Pollard–Millet decisions. Earlier publication statements below document the frozen version 1.0 history. This book has 1 approved running-text revision and 1 annotation-only decision; every other running passage and all citation identifiers remain unchanged. See _docs/DEH_POLLARD_MILLET_EDITORIAL_20261025.md and the accompanying sixteen-entry decision log. The Latin, Millet transcription, Style Guide v1.0 and TEI Technical Specification v1.3 are unchanged.

English translation prepared for LatinJosephus.org, 16 September 2026. Complete Book II first draft: [II.1.1]–[II.18.1], exactly seventy-three aligned citation units. Tranche 4 adds [II.14.1]–[II.18.1], units num57–num73. Working v0.6 preserves v0.5 apart from the five approved prose revisions PR01–PR05; PR01 and PR02 use the editor’s modified wording. D1 at [II.2.4] and D2 at [II.9.1] remain resolved by editorial approval with correction; their approved wording is retained exactly. D3 at [II.12.1], D4 at [II.12.2] and D5 at [II.13.1] are resolved by editorial approval; working wording approved exactly, without correction. The whole-book philological audit is complete; all human decisions D1–D6 and C1/R1–R3 are incorporated. D6 adopts the locative “There” from the editor’s DEH apparatus evidence ubi (s. quibus) B without altering the frozen Latin. No unresolved Book II philological, interpretative or prose/rhetorical decision remains after the 16 September 2026 editorial adjudication; see DEH_English_Book_II_Philological_Decisions_2026-09-16.md, DEH_English_Book_II_Prose_Editorial_Decisions_2026-09-16.md and DEH_English_Book_II_Review_Register_v8.md. The whole-book prose/rhetorical audit and editorial adjudication are complete; PR01–PR05 are incorporated. Final proofing, human adjudication and publication-layer regression testing are complete. Version 1.0 is the frozen Book II publication text; its running English is identical to Release Candidate 1. The canonical DEH Latin and English Release Candidate 1 were successfully served and regression-tested together in the local successor to LatinJosephus.org on 17 September 2026.

Frozen English Book I version 1.0 supplies style and implementation precedent only and is not altered. Fragment-only sameAs values resolve against the separately held canonical Latin document under the project convention. Visible num labels are copied exactly. No English pb or lb milestones are included. Constituted supplied text is translated, excluded text is not; the empty unclear marker at [II.14.4] remains intact in the Latin and its consequence is documented as D6 rather than supplied with conjectural wording. Long periods may become multiple sentences within their unchanged aligned paragraph; direct and indirect discourse remain distinguished. div2.head: Book II
div2.p: [II.1.1] Once Herod was buried, the people freely brought out their judgements, as is usual against the dead: he had been oppressive and intolerable to them; he had exercised unjust rule over his fellow citizens, a tyrant, not a king; a murderer of his own kin at home, a plunderer in public, he had left nothing to anyone. Tribute had been added, everything exhausted, foreigners enriched and Jews emptied of their wealth. He had brought an enemy into the temple and contaminated all its sacred things with sacrilege. Happy were those who had died, since the living never lacked torments. In a few years under Herod’s rule, after their captivity had been cast off, Judaea had endured more evils than it had borne in captivity itself under a barbarian enemy, when the kings of the Babylonians ruled over them. Exile under those kings had been more tolerable than dwelling at home under Herod: those kings had sent them back to their own homes, but he had driven them away. He had been more merciless than Darius, prouder than Artaxerxes, more rapacious than the Medes. They had hoped for an end to their evils, that they might leave exile if he ended his days, but Archelaus had added himself to the misery of their slavery as a self-appointed successor, reproducing Herod and adding new evils. It was a misery in kingdoms that a master was chosen, and a greater misery that he was imposed upon the unwilling. It seemed a consolation in slavery if they chose their own master, since he became kinder if rule was conferred upon him, prouder if he usurped it. Archelaus would therefore be far more intolerable than Herod, since the former had assumed kingship, while the latter had received it.

[II.1.2] These things were not only discussed frequently in Judaea but also thrown in Archelaus’s face at Rome, as he stood before Caesar and the senate and his accusers pleaded their case. There was a long contest there over confirming or revoking Archelaus’s kingship. When a place had been assigned for the hearing in the temple of Apollo, which Caesar had founded and embellished with many ornaments, Salome’s son Antipater, a powerful speaker, developed the arguments we have given above and many others. He marvelled that Archelaus made a show of seeking kingship from Caesar, when by a reckless usurpation he had long since acted as king in Judaea without consulting Caesar. For what else were the golden chair and the diadem brought before him but the insignia of kingship? With what arrogance had he presumed to sit upon the royal throne? From a lofty seat he greeted the people, surrounded by close ranks of soldiers. The diadem was brought out according to the custom and practice of emperors, although it ought to have been reserved for Caesar’s judgement, both because of the authority of Roman rule and because of the legal force of the will. For Herod could not have forestalled Caesar or the senate in a matter in which he himself had either received authority from the senate or received it back from Caesar. In his earlier will he had expressed a sufficiently clear indication of his own wishes, declaring with sound judgement and considered counsel that Antipas should succeed him in the kingdom. In his later will he had reserved everything for Caesar’s judgement, although his body was already failing and, anxious at his mortal danger and no longer capable of any judgement or counsel, he had dictated what was put before him rather than what he himself thought. The man who had forestalled the grant of rule had therefore pronounced upon himself that he did not deserve to be appointed to the kingdom by your judgement, Caesar; for, had he been conscious of his own merit, he would have hastened to ask rather than to seize. By usurping what depended upon a petition instead of petitioning for it, men commonly prejudiced their case even in financial disputes, so that litigants who reversed the proper order lost their suit. Here, however, the charge concerned no monetary gain: the rights of Roman rule had been violated, its dignity despised, its authority spurned. The senate of the Roman curia, accustomed to give and take away kingdoms, had been judged unworthy to preserve, together with Caesar, its ancient prerogative of conferring rule. What would he, who had grown insolent even before his reign, do once he began to reign lawfully? Very many had also been killed because they had sought relief for their exhausted resources and a lightening of tribute. War had been imposed upon those asking for a remedy; nine thousand Jews had been killed in the very celebration of Passover, revered among their people; human beings had been sacrificed in place of animals; the blood of the consecrated, who had gathered for the temple’s festivals, had been poured out—a pitiable spectacle. Anyone who surveyed the slaughter of the dead would think that the Babylonians had returned. How much more cruel were deeds committed by a fellow citizen that would be judged full of monstrous savagery and impiety even in a barbarian enemy! This was the dole given to the citizens; with this sacrifice Archelaus had commended the beginnings of his kingship. Caesar and the senate ought to pity the remnants of Judaea, once supported by free peoples, which now wished for slavery, if only it could endure a tolerable slavery under a just king. Archelaus was far from possessing the right to rule, since among the Jews kingship belonged to no one except a man descended from Judah, as the law said. But this man, of Idumaean stock, with no connection by birth to the royal line, had crept into an honour not owed to him. Antipater had been grandfather to both the speaker and Archelaus, outstanding in wealth and powerful in other accomplishments, especially in his friendship with the Romans, and proven in war to the elder Caesar. Although he could have claimed kingship for himself, he had never sought it; indeed, he had preferred to defend it for others rather than obtain it for himself. He had deservedly been regarded as the best of fathers, having won freedom for Judaea by his wounds, without bringing it into slavery. Herod had aspired to kingship through the testimony of Antony, his father’s guest-friend. From that time the fortunes of the Jews had declined: Herod had acted as an enemy, not a ruler. Since he himself had been an adulterer of kingship, how could a lawful king have been created by him? They did not, however, plead to be free of kingship, but asked to be under Roman rule, whose favour had already been secured for them in the days of the Maccabees. Through the later usurpation of kingship they had declined so far that they were much inferior to those against whom they had sought alliance with Rome. Finally, he said that they begged, “Grant Judaea government by a provincial governor on the same terms as Syria, so that our devotion may be put to the test: whether we, who are called seditious and rebellious, can obey moderate judges.”
